Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:25: Also included in this is what I explained, that "the Glorious One" indicates that He is the source of souls; for since "glorious" indicates the totality of the thirty-two paths, among these thirty-two is the path of the creation of man - "and God created man in His image" - and man is the soul, which is called "Adam," for the body is called "the flesh of man," as it is said (Exodus 30:32), "upon the flesh of man it shall not be poured."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:26: "And awesome" [ve-hanora], according to this explanation, means that because of the revelation of His glory to us, we fear before Him - like the parable of the king's servants who see the king's face and fear him because he is before them, unlike one who does not see the king's face or his dwelling place, who has no fear of the king. And so said our father Jacob, peace be upon him (Genesis 28:17), "how awesome is this place! this is none other than the house of God" - for it is from its being the house of God that it instills awe.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:27: Among the ways of one who fears the king is not to lift his eyes before him; and so, at the vision of the [burning] bush, it says of Moses (Exodus 3:6), "and Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God." From this it follows that a person should not walk with an upright, haughty bearing, so as not to remove awe from himself; and this was the virtue of Rav, peace be upon him - one of the ten qualities he had was that he would not look further than four cubits, the reason being so as not to remove the awe of the Shechinah from himself; and further, so that he would not see any transgression [at a time when he was unable to protest, in the sense of (Psalms 119:37), "turn away my eyes from seeing vanity"].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:28: In particular, at the time of prayer, one must believe that His glory fills the world, and should feel awe and shame before Him and cast his eyes downward, as our Sages, of blessed memory, explained (Yevamot 105b): "one who prays should cast his eyes downward and his heart upward." And a person should imagine that if he were seeing a great light, so bright that it would darken his eyes, he surely would not gaze at it - as is said in Parashat Bereshit (4a), in the story of Rabbi Chiya, when he saw Rabbi Shimon [bar Yochai] after his passing: a voice went forth and said, "lower your eye, do not raise your head and do not look" - he lowered his eyes and saw a light shining from afar. And likewise at the passing of Rashbi, peace be upon him (Ha'azinu 291b), Rabbi Abba said, "I did not raise my head, for the light was so great that I could not gaze upon it." Similarly, when a person prays and considers that the Glorious Name is before him, who is the source of illumination without limit, it is fitting that he should feel shame and lower his eyes before the glory of the LORD.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:29: Likewise, in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (chapter 4), it is said that the Chayot stand beside the Throne of His Glory, and even though they do not know the place of His glory, they nevertheless stand in dread and fear; in these words, in chapter four: "and the Chayot stand beside the Throne of His Glory, and they do not know the place of His glory, and the Chayot stand in dread and fear, trembling and quaking, and from the sweat of their faces a river of fire is drawn forth and goes out before Him, as it is said (Daniel 7:10), 'a river of fire flowed and went forth from before Him.' Two seraphim stand, one to the right of the Holy One, blessed be He, and one to His left, six wings each, with two he covers his face so that they should not look upon the face of the Shechinah," and so on - to the extent relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:30: One may also explain "the Glorious and Awesome One" according to what is explained in the Tikkunim: that just as there are thirty-two [occurrences of] "Elohim" in the work of creation, so there are, correspondingly, thirty-two occurrences of "the LORD" at known points derived from the verses, as is explained there; and we find, then, that there is nothing in the world that is not stamped with the Name "the LORD" and the Name "Elohim" together, as one. If so, "the Glorious One" is so called from the side of the Name "the LORD," for the reason I explained above, and "the Awesome One" from the side of the Name "Elohim," for most fear comes from judgment; and this is [the meaning of] (Deuteronomy 28:58), "this glorious and awesome [Name], the LORD your God" - for "the LORD" [Havayah] is "glorious" from the side of kindness, and "your God" [Elohim] from the side of judgment.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:31: With this we may understand the verse (ibid. 4:39), "and you shall know this day, and take it to your heart, that the LORD, He is God, in the heavens above," and so on. The matter is that the perfection of kindness comes only when it comprises judgment within it, and there is no perfection to judgment except with mercy; and this is [the meaning of] that "the LORD," who is the master of kindness and mercy, is "God," comprising judgment within Him - and likewise "God" is "the LORD." The manner in which "Elohim" [God] is found within "the LORD" is explained in the Tikkunim (73b): for "the LORD" spelled out in full - Yud, Heh, Vav, Heh - adds up to Mah [forty-five]; and when these letters, Mem and Heh, are found, they add up to the numerical value of "Elohim." And because the Name "the LORD" comprises "Elohim" within it, therefore the entire work of creation, accomplished through the thirty-two paths, came about through both these Names together; and this is [the meaning of] "that the LORD, He is God, in the heavens above" - meaning that the heavens above and the earth below were all created through Him, and there is none else.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:32: As for how fear results from this for a person - the matter is that what we explained above, in chapter one, in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, peace be upon him, that the essence of fear is to fear the Name because He is great and dominant, the foundation and root of all worlds, and everything before Him is accounted as nothing - all of this our holy Torah revealed in its brief words by saying "the glorious and awesome." In "the Glorious One" it indicates that He is great and dominant, the foundation and root of all worlds - for through the thirty-two paths His greatness and dominion are revealed to the lower beings, and likewise in this He is the foundation and root of all worlds, for through the thirty-two paths life spreads to all the lower beings. And through the Name "the LORD," life spreads through all existing things, which were created through Him - in the manner that He is "great and dominant" - so that He is found to be the foundation and root of all worlds.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:33: "And awesome" is [that] "everything before Him is accounted as nothing." And what is explained there, at the end of chapter one, regarding this matter, is the fear that comes from judgment - that when the Holy One, blessed be He, does good to a person, and he transgresses His will, one must fear, for the King, even though at present He does not show him an angry countenance, nevertheless will exact payment from him afterward; and this is [the meaning of] "your God" - in the manner explained in the Zohar, Parashat Beshalach (51b, 60b). And I shall elaborate further on this, with God's help.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:34: It seems to me that this fear is what Rashbi attributed, in the Zohar (Naso 122b) and in the Tikkunim (129a), to the Yud of "Yirah" [fear] and the Heh of "Ahavah" [love] - and the matter of love will be explained in the next Gate, with God's help. But as for attributing fear to the Yud, which is "the beginning of wisdom" [reishit chochmah] - this is according to what I explained, that since He is "great and dominant, the foundation and root of all worlds," everything is found within "the LORD," and the Name "the LORD" is in Chochmah [Wisdom], for the entire Yud is "the LORD." If so, there lies the essence of fear - especially when we consider what Scripture says (Psalms 104:24), "You have made them all in wisdom" - and this is the secret of the [primordial] thought that sends forth life into all the worlds; and this is [the meaning of] the verse (Proverbs 14:27), "the fear of the LORD is a source of life," as it is known that it is the source of life for all the worlds.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:35: And because it might seem difficult, at first glance, to say of Chochmah [Wisdom] that it is the foundation for all the worlds, we found support for this in Parashat Vayikra (10b), in these words: "we have learned, in the Book of Enoch, that at the time they showed him the wisdom of the supernal secrets, and he saw the Tree of the Garden of Eden, they showed him wisdom through a supernal secret, and he saw that all the worlds were bound one to another; he asked them upon what they stood, and they told him: they all stand upon the Yud, and from it they were built and drawn forth in sequence; and he saw that they all trembled from fear of their Master, and were all called by His Name" - to this point. And afterward they said that the supernal thorn [crown-tip] upon the Yud is the fear of all.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:36: Regarding the greatness of Chochmah's magnitude, it is explained in the book Brit Menuchah, in these words: "the vastness of the host of heaven is without limit, for a single angel named Uriel spans, in a single stride, from the tenth sphere to the earth, as it is said, 'now I have come'; and if a single angel such as this [can span] nine spheres, which are not so vast, how much more so Yaho'el, who is above him, before whom Uriel appears like a mere youth; and Yaho'el, before Shemu'el, is as nothing; and these three princes, before the Da'at [Knowledge] that spreads forth from the offspring of the intellect, are accounted as nothing; and so too the intellect compared to Binah, and Binah compared to Chochmah - and Chochmah, whose likeness is that she is the mother of all the luminaries and of the intellect of all the spheres and their hosts, and of the luminaries that sustain their creatures, and of all the treasuries - all these are accounted before her as nothing, for she reclines in the bosom of the King and is the King's minister. And as the sages who delve deeply into Chochmah, to know her root, perceive - that all the luminaries and their hosts, and the world and its hosts, and the depths and the fish of the sea and all the waters beneath the heavens - Chochmah hovers over them all, and none of them is visible [in comparison to her], and they are all accounted, compared to Chochmah, like a small bowl with no water in it. And when they delved deeply to know this great Chochmah, they said: how great is the Master of all worlds, that such a light spreads forth from Him!" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:37: Concerning this supernal fear, it is said in the Tikkunim (126b), on [the phrase] "and their height, and they were dreadful [ve-yirah] to them" [Ezekiel 1:18] - regarding the letters, vowel-points, and cantillation marks, which are Binah, Chochmah, and Keter - and they said, "'and they were dreadful to them' - this is the crown [Keter], where the cantillation marks are" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:38: Because this fear is in a hidden place, it is written afterward (Deuteronomy 28:59), "then the LORD will make your plagues wondrous [ve-hifla]" - and it is known that the term "wonder" [pele] applies only to this place [Chochmah], as is explained in the Zohar, Parashat Tzav (31a), on the verse (Isaiah 9:5), "wondrous [pele] counselor."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:39: Concerning this fear it is said (Proverbs 10:27), "the fear of the LORD adds days" - this being the fear that comes on account of "the LORD," as we have explained the four aspects concerning fear, all of which depend on "the LORD," who is "great and dominant, the foundation and root," and so on, and "everything before Him is accounted as nothing." And above [in Chochmah] is the place of the addition of life, as is explained in the Zohar (Tosefta, Chukat 274b), on the verse (Isaiah 38:5), "behold, I will add to your days." Therefore it does not say "the fear of God [Elohim] adds days," for the fear of Elohim is a fear arising from judgment, and it is in the place of smallness and contraction, and is not among the degrees of the esteemed fear that adds days; but this fear [the fear of "the LORD"] is fear of His greatness, blessed be He, arising from "the LORD" - for this Name formed him [man] with his two hundred and forty-eight limbs and his soul, and is imprinted upon him in every single limb, and he fears to sin before the King who is before him - like the servants of the king who see the king's seal and fear that very seal as they would fear the king himself, as is explained in the Tikkunim (65b), on the verse (Song of Songs 8:6), "set me as a seal."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:40: We find, then, three aspects in the verse [Proverbs 10:27]: the first is the fear of Elohim, which does not add days, but only [preserves] the days already allotted to him from the day of his creation. The furthest extreme among these degrees is the fear of "the LORD," which adds days. And "the years of the wicked," who have no fear at all, "shall be shortened" from the years allotted to them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:41: There is yet a fourth way to explain "the glorious and awesome," following what is explained in Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Kedoshim 82a) concerning "honor your father and your mother." It is explained there that Chochmah is called "kavod" [honor/glory] because she is a throne for the supernal Keter, to serve beneath it and to carry out its utterance through her thirty-two paths; in these words, in brief: "and because it carries out His utterance and command without delay, through the thirty-two paths by which the entire work of creation was made, it is called 'kavod,' as it is said, 'and in His Temple all say, glory [kavod]' (Psalms 29:9)," and so on - to the extent relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:42: And further there, shortly after, concerning the honor of father and mother: "the honor of his father and mother is to carry out their command, and their command consists of the positive commandments; and the masters of the Mishnah have already established that there is one who is commanded and performs, and this is why it is 'we will do and we will hear' - and this is the honor of father and mother, that a father commands his child to do such-and-such, and he does it immediately, without any delay at all" - to this point. And it is explained there, shortly after, that "every man shall fear [tira'u] his mother and his father" [Leviticus 19:3] - the fear is to take care not to transgress a negative commandment.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:43: In this manner we may also explain "the glorious and awesome": "the Glorious One" - that all creatures are subjugated to His utterance, to honor Him and do His will; and "the Awesome One" - that all fear to transgress His commandments, as the prophet said (Jeremiah 5:22), "will you not fear Me, says the LORD, will you not tremble before Me, who have placed the sand as a bound for the sea, an everlasting decree, that it cannot pass over it," and so on. This verse will be explained, with God's help, in the next chapter.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 2:44: One may also offer an additional refinement, according to what is explained in the Tikkunim (5a): that the Name "the LORD" comprises the negative and positive commandments - "Shem" [Name, i.e., Shin-Mem] together with Yud-Heh [make] three hundred sixty-five [the negative commandments], and "Zachar" [male, i.e., Zayin-Chaf-Reish] together with Vav-Heh [make] two hundred forty-eight [the positive commandments]. If so, we find that "the LORD" is called both "glorious" and "awesome": "glorious," for He is the source of the positive commandments, in the secret of Vav-Heh; and "awesome," from the side of the negative commandments, which are Yud-Heh.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:1: Since our discussion in the previous chapter, concerning "the glorious and awesome," preceded us - that among the particulars of fear is that, since all creatures are subjugated to His utterance and fear to transgress His command, so too a person must fear and feel shame not to transgress the command of his Creator, and this is the degree of fear that comes from shame - we have seen fit to append this chapter, to expand upon this matter through the words of our Sages, of blessed memory.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:2: Our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Sifrei, Parashat Ha'azinu), in these words: "'Give ear, O heavens' - the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses: tell Israel, look at the heavens which I created to serve you - have they ever changed their custom, or has the sun's orb ever gone forth in the west? As it is said (Ecclesiastes 1:5), 'the sun rises and the sun sets'; and not only that, but it rejoices to do My will, as it is said (Psalms 19:6), 'and it is like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber.' 'And let the earth hear the words of my mouth' - look at the earth which I created to serve you - has it ever changed its custom? Have you ever sown and it did not sprout, or sown wheat and it brought forth barley? Has this cow ever said, I will not thresh and I will not plow? Has this donkey ever said, I will not carry a load and I will not walk? And so too regarding the sea, it says (Jeremiah 5:22), 'will you not fear Me, says the LORD, will you not tremble before Me, who have placed the sand as a bound for the sea' - from the hour I decreed upon it, has it ever changed its custom and said, I will rise up and flood the world? - as it is said (Job 38:10-11), 'and I broke for it My bound,' and so on, 'and said, thus far shall you come and no farther.' And not only that, but it is distressed and cannot do so, as it is said (Jeremiah 5:22), 'and though they toss, they cannot prevail.' Now, is this not an argument from minor to major: if these, which were made neither for reward nor for punishment - if they merit, they receive no reward, and if they sin, they receive no punishment, and they have no pity on their sons and daughters - have not changed their custom; you, who if you merit receive reward, and if you sin receive punishment, and who have pity on your sons and daughters, how much more so should you not change your customs!" - to the extent relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:3: The pious master, author of Chovot HaLevavot (Duties of the Heart) (Gate of Self-Reckoning, chapter 3), wrote something related to this; I have seen fit to cite some of his words, in these words: "The sixth [reckoning]: that a person consider with his soul, when he feels his character traits inclining toward rebelling against the Creator and breaking His covenant, and let him ponder in his soul and pass before his heart all that he has grasped with his senses of the roots and branches of the world, its simple and composite parts, its upper and lower realms - that everything stands by His word and keeps the covenant of the Name; has he ever seen anything among them depart from the bond of service to God, blessed be He, or rebel against His word and break His covenant? And let him consider the limbs of man - if they were to transgress God's covenant within man, and his natural limbs, meant for motion, were to rest, or those meant to rest were to move, or if the senses did not bring to him what they were commanded to bring, his constitution would be corrupted, his composition disordered, and his governance nullified. How, then, should a person not be ashamed to transgress the covenant of his God, in a world where [even] the sea does not transgress the covenant of its God - he, and the helpers who are obligated in His service and in bearing his affairs, namely his limbs? Do you not know that God stipulated in His faithful Torah that everything in the world would be at your disposal and by your will, if you serve Him; and that He would transgress your will when you transgress His word - as is explained in the passage 'if you walk in My statutes'" - to this point. And I have abbreviated some of his words, so as not to lengthen unduly.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:4: Now, in this manner one may also explain the verse (Jeremiah 5:22), "will you not fear Me, says the LORD, will you not tremble before Me, who have placed the sand as a bound for the sea," and so on. For since the sea is a physical thing without sensation - and how much more so the other creatures - yet they do the will of the Creator, blessed be He, how should a person not fear to transgress the will of his Creator with his limbs, which were created to serve the Creator? For the heart is the essential organ created to fear the Creator, since fear depends on the heart, as it is said (Jeremiah 32:40), "and I will put My fear in their hearts"; and further on, the prophet says (ibid. 5:24), "neither say they in their heart, let us now fear the LORD," and so on - and even so, it was through it [the heart] that they transgressed the will of the Creator, as it is said (ibid. 5:23), "but this people has a stubborn and rebellious heart," and so on. How much more so the other limbs, through which they certainly transgressed the will of the Creator.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:5: I have seen fit to examine these verses closely and to explain them, with God's help, since they bear on the matter of the fear of the LORD. One point to examine: the apparent repetition in the verse, "will you not fear Me, says the LORD, will you not tremble before Me" - which appears to repeat the same matter in different words. And what is meant by "fear Me," and afterward "tremble before Me" [literally, "before My face"] - for it seems that both are the same. And afterward it returns and says, "neither say they in their heart, let us now fear the LORD," and so on - what is the point of this second [mention of] fear? Why not combine them and teach them together, saying, "will you not fear Me... who have placed the sand as a bound for the sea... and who gives you the early and late rain in its season," and so on? Furthermore, above, in the first verse, it mentions fear plainly, "will you not fear Me," without mentioning the heart, while in the second [mention of] fear, it mentions the heart - one must understand the reason for this.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:6: To resolve, in general, why two [instances of] fear are mentioned: one may say that the first fear corresponds to the negative commandments, as the plain sense of the verse indicates, saying, "will you not tremble before Me, who have placed the sand as a bound for the sea... and it cannot pass over it," and so on - "but you transgress the bound of the Torah," as it says, "but this people has a stubborn and rebellious heart," and so on. And the second fear corresponds to the positive commandments - that one must fear and say in his heart: since the Holy One, blessed be He, does good for us, giving the early and late rain, and keeping for us the appointed weeks of harvest, so too we shall keep and perform every single commandment in its proper time, as He has commanded us; for through this we lend power above, as in (Deuteronomy 33:26), "who rides the heavens to your help" - and the opposite, Heaven forfend (ibid. 32:18), "you have forgotten the Rock who bore you." And as our Sages, of blessed memory, explained in the Pesikta, cited in the Yalkut, in the explanation of the verse "you have forgotten the Rock who bore you," in these words: "when Israel does the will of the Omnipresent, they add strength and might, as it is said (Numbers 14:17), 'and now, please, let the power of the LORD be great'; and when they anger Him, it is as though, 'you have forgotten the Rock who bore you'" - to the extent relevant here. And they elaborate further there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:7: With this we may also resolve why the heart is not mentioned in the first [instance of] fear: because that fear is not in the heart alone, but encompasses all the limbs of a person, who transgress the entire Torah - for each and every limb must fear not to transgress the commandment that depends on that limb, just as the sea keeps its bound and does not transgress it, in the manner explained in Chovot HaLevavot. However, the second fear, which concerns the positive commandments, depends on the heart, for it is for a person to consider in his heart the good the Creator has done for him, as we have explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:8: And in this manner [we understand] the fear that is in the heart - it is known what is explained in the Tikkunim (24a), that "lev" [heart] used plainly refers to the heart, "from within the heart it knows," and so on; and this is [the meaning of] "fear enters his heart," which is the secret of Heh-Yud from Elohim; and the fear used plainly, which encompasses the negative commandments, is the lower fear. This is what appears to me on this matter.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:9: Regarding the repetition in the verse, "will you not fear Me, says the LORD, will you not tremble before Me [mipanai]" - the explanation is: "will you not fear Me" refers to His own essence, which is hidden and cannot be grasped by you; "says the LORD" [ne'um Hashem] - for this Name, "the LORD," is called so, blessed be He, from the aspect that He brought all existing things into being, and His acts of bringing-into-being that He created indicate His greatness, and that He, blessed be He, created them, as explained in chapter one. "Will you not tremble before Me [mipanai]" - meaning "from before Me," from the aspect of His face that is revealed to you; and this is like the parable of one who hears a report of the king, as opposed to one who sees his face - for one who sees his face fears the king more, and trembling seizes him like a woman in labor; and this is [the meaning of] "will you not tremble before Me."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:10: These two aspects are both found in the sea, and both are found in man. Regarding the sea, it is already known, from the passage we cited at the beginning of the chapter, that the Holy One, blessed be He, decreed upon it that it should not go beyond its bound, and the sand is its bound; and behold, the king's decree that He decreed upon it at the time of the world's creation is a hidden aspect, and the sea keeps the king's command that He commanded it so many years ago, even though the king now commands it nothing further - and this is the aspect of "will you not fear Me." And corresponding to "before Me" [mipanai] is that the sea sees the sand around it and knows that the Holy One, blessed be He, placed this bound for it, and it does not transgress it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:11: Corresponding to these two aspects mentioned, there are corresponding aspects in man regarding the Torah: for the Torah and the commandments given to us in the Five Books of the Torah are the bound that we constantly see, like the sand that is around the sea; and this is, in truth, the face of the King - except that we do not actually see the King's face, but the Torah is the stamped image of the King. However, we did see the King Himself at the time of the giving of the Torah, as I explained in chapter one; and this is [the meaning of] "will you not fear Me" - for it should suffice for us [to keep] the first command from the King Himself, along with the boundary He set for us afterward regarding the commandments - just as the sea was commanded only once, and it stands by that command in its observance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:12: One may also say that the boundary that the Holy One, blessed be He, created within man himself is the good inclination [yetzer tov]. This is what our Sages, of blessed memory, explained: that there are two chambers in the heart, one full of blood, which is the dwelling of the evil inclination, and the other a chamber without blood, which is the dwelling of the good inclination. Now, when the waves of the evil inclination roar to transgress the Torah, the good inclination stands opposite it and counsels it to return to good; and there is no wicked person to whom thoughts of repentance do not come before he commits the transgression, but his inclination entices him, and afterward he regrets it - as they said (Akeidah, Gate 67), "the wicked are full of regrets." And therefore the verse says (Jeremiah 5:23), "but this people has a stubborn and rebellious heart; they have turned aside and gone" - for they turned aside from the boundary that is in their heart, which is the good inclination that warns them, and they went outward. And this is what our Sages, of blessed memory, said in the first chapter of Bava Batra (16a): "I created the evil inclination, I created the good inclination; I created the evil inclination, I created a remedy against it, which is the Torah."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:13: In this manner one may also find an allusion in the repetition of the verse: "will you not fear Me, says the LORD" corresponds to the Name "the LORD"; "will you not tremble before Me [mipanai]" corresponds to the Name Adonai, which is [the aspect of] "face" [panim], and this is the secret of "the whole earth is full of His glory," as is explained in the Tikkunim. And corresponding to these two aspects in the sea: the first, corresponding to the Name Adonai, is "the sand [as] a bound for the sea, an everlasting decree, that it cannot pass over it" - this being the revealed aspect. And corresponding to the hidden aspect is (Jeremiah 5:22), "and though they toss, they cannot prevail; though its waves roar, they cannot pass over it" - and at first glance, "though they toss, they cannot prevail" seems superfluous. Rather, the matter may be understood from what is explained (Noach 69b), on the verse (Psalms 89:10), "You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, You still them" - for when the sea is at the height of its fury, a thread of kindness is drawn through it to calm it from its rage and fury; and so it says there, "'You still them' [teshabchem]" - "You break them to return them to their place" - and because it is the Holy One, blessed be He, who sends forth this thread, it is therefore attributed to the Name "the LORD."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:14: With this we may understand the passage from the Sifrei that we cited at the beginning of the chapter, which said, "and not only that, but it is distressed and cannot do so, as it is said, 'though they toss, they cannot prevail.'"
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:15: Corresponding to these two aspects explained, there are corresponding aspects in man: the first is the inner spirit within him, which is the secret of "who forms the spirit of man within him" (Zechariah 12:1), as is explained in the Zohar (Miketz 197a); and the second is the aspect of the garment, which is the body in which the spirit is clothed. And when a person considers this - that his spirit and all his limbs are made and directed by the counsel of the Supernal Court - he must fear lest he blemish his limbs or his spirit, as our Sages, of blessed memory, explained on the verse (Ecclesiastes 2:12), "that which they have already made [asuhu]" - in these words: "'asuhu' [they made him/it] - it is not written 'asahu' [He made him/it], but 'asuhu' [they made him/it] - as if to say, the King of kings of kings and His court took counsel over each and every one of your limbs, and set you upon your foundation, as it is said (Deuteronomy 32:6), 'He made you and established you'" - to this point, cited in the Yalkut on Job (remez 914), on the verse (Job 26:13), "by His spirit the heavens are calmed [or: made fair]." Thus one aspect of the fear that comes from shame has been explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:16: There is a second aspect: when the Holy One, blessed be He, bestows upon a person wealth, honor, possessions, children, and the like of this world's goods, he must fear lest sin be caused - as is said of our father Jacob, peace be upon him (Genesis 32:8), "and Jacob was greatly afraid" - and our Sages, of blessed memory, explained (Berachot 4a) that he said, "perhaps sin will be caused." For Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi raised a contradiction: it is written (Genesis 28:15), "and behold, I am with you, and I will keep you wherever you go," yet it is written, "and Jacob was greatly afraid" - he said, perhaps sin will be caused, as it is taught: "'till Your people pass over, O LORD; till the people pass over whom You have acquired' (Exodus 15:16) - 'till Your people pass over, O LORD' refers to the first entry [into the land, under Joshua]; 'till the people pass over whom You have acquired' refers to the second entry [under Ezra]." From here the Sages said: Israel deserved to have a miracle performed for them in the days of Ezra just as was done for them in the days of Joshua, but sin was the cause [that prevented it] - to the extent relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:17: Know that this matter of fear that I explained, "perhaps sin will be caused," concerns the blemish in the attribute [Shechinah] that accompanies us in exile; and for this reason he brought proof from the Baraita that in the days of Ezra sin was the cause, and the cause of the sin was that they blemished [the covenant] through foreign women; and he brought this Baraita to teach us the secret of where sin causes its blemish - as Rashbi explains in Parashat Ki Tisa (Zohar 194b). And the matter of where sin causes its blemish here is as Rashbi explains in Parashat Vayikra (20a), on the verse (Psalms 32:5), "I acknowledged my sin to You."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:18: With this we may understand the fear of "perhaps sin will be caused," as Rashbi explains in Parashat Bereshit (12a), in these words: "Rabbi Elazar said: fear should not be forgotten in any of the commandments, and how much more so in this commandment is fear needed, to cleave to this. How does one cleave [to it]? Love is on one side, the good side, as has been said - that He gives wealth and good, length of days, children and sustenance; then fear must be aroused, to fear lest one cause sin - and therefore it is written (Proverbs 28:14), 'happy is the man who fears always,' for fear is thereby included within love. And so, on the other side, the side of harsh judgment, fear must likewise be aroused there - when one sees that harsh judgment rests upon him, then fear should be aroused, and he should fear his Master as is fitting, and not harden his heart; and therefore it is written [ibid.], 'but he who hardens his heart shall fall into evil' - on that other side, which is called 'evil.' We find, then, that fear is found bound to both sides, and comprises them both, and this is complete love, as is fitting" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:19: Now, what he said, "fear should not be forgotten," and so on, was explained above, on the previous page, that he said "Bereishit" alludes to fear, which is the opening and gateway to all the commandments; and he said that this fear is "perhaps sin will be caused" - this is the secret to which I have alluded.
